name: Thorny devil  -  drinking through skin & the false head
scope: Headline: the thorny devil (Moloch horridus) of Australia's desert drinks with its skin — grooves between its spines wick dew and puddle-water up to its mouth by capillary action, so it can drink standing in damp sand or even off morning dew on its own back. Other distinct wonders: the decoy 'false head' — a knobby lump on the back of its neck it presents to predators by tucking its real head down; its slow, jerky, rocking walk (a camouflage gait that mimics wind-blown debris); ant specialist, eating thousands of tiny ants one at a time.
source: Peer-reviewed studies on capillary/integumentary water transport in Moloch horridus (Bentley & Blumer 1962; Sherbrooke et al.); Australian herpetology references.
framing_note: Anchor = the thorny devil, every rung a fact about IT. Lead with the skin-drinking wonder (capillary grooves wick water to the mouth) — vivid adaptation, top of the Wonder ladder. Do NOT restate 'it drinks through its skin' on a later rung; each rung a DISTINCT fact: the false head (named decoy), the rocking camouflage walk (vivid action), the one-ant-at-a-time diet (constructed number only if it lands as WHAT?!). Never anthropomorphize the decoy as 'trickery' stated as intent — describe the behavior. Real binomial Moloch horridus.

name: Marine iguana  -  the only sea-going lizard
scope: Headline: the marine iguana (Amblyrhynchus cristatus) of the Galapagos is the world's only lizard that forages in the ocean, diving and clinging to rocks to graze algae underwater. Other distinct wonders: it sneezes salt — special nasal glands concentrate swallowed seawater salt and it expels it in a crusty white spray; it basks black to reheat after cold dives (cold-blooded, so it must sun itself between dives); in lean years it can shrink its own skeleton, getting physically shorter, then regrow — documented by Wikelski.
source: Galapagos herpetology literature; Wikelski et al. on body-length shrinkage during El Nino; salt-gland physiology studies.
framing_note: Anchor = marine iguana. Lead with 'only sea-going lizard' (recognition hook + wonder). Distinct rungs: salt-sneezing (vivid action, named salt glands), the black basking reheat (cold-blooded consequence), the shrink-and-regrow skeleton (jaw-dropping, well-documented). One wonder per rung; don't restate the diving on multiple rungs. Real binomial Amblyrhynchus cristatus.

name: Basilisk  -  the lizard that runs on water
scope: Headline: the basilisk (genus Basiliscus), the 'Jesus Christ lizard,' sprints ACROSS the surface of water on its hind legs — slapping the water fast enough that a trapped air pocket holds its splayed, fringed toes up before they sink. Other distinct wonders: it only pulls this off while young/light (small ones cross water; big adults sink and swim); the escape is a predator-dodge (it bolts across a stream to leave a land predator stranded); fringed toe flaps that unfurl to maximize the slapping surface.
source: Biomechanics studies of basilisk water-running (Glasheen & McMahon 1996; Hsieh & Lauder); Central American herpetology.
framing_note: Anchor = basilisk lizard. Lead with the water-running wonder — but the ANSWER at each rung must be a DIFFERENT facet of it, not a restated headline: rung on the MECHANISM (slap traps air under fringed toes), rung on the SIZE limit (only the light young manage it), rung on WHY (escaping a land predator). Fringed-toe adaptation is a distinct object-rung. Avoid the myth/symbol angle (basilisk-of-legend) — that belongs to another bank; keep it pure biology. Genus Basiliscus.

name: Draco  -  the gliding lizard on rib-wings
scope: Headline: Draco lizards ('flying dragons' of SE Asia) glide tree-to-tree on wings made of skin stretched over hugely elongated RIBS that swing out like a folding fan. Other distinct wonders: they steer and can glide 30+ metres between trunks, banking with body and tail; a bright throat flap (the dewlap/gular flag) they flash to rival males and mates; they almost never come to the ground, living, feeding on ants, and gliding entirely in the canopy.
source: Herpetology and gliding-locomotion literature on genus Draco (McGuire & Dudley on glide performance).
framing_note: Anchor = Draco. Lead with the wing-from-ribs wonder (the specific, jaw-dropping structural fact — elongated ribs, not limbs). Distinct rungs: the glide distance/steering (vivid action), the throat-flag dewlap (named display object), canopy-only life. Keep it mini — don't pad. Don't conflate with 'flying snake' or flying frog (separate ladders). Genus Draco.

name: Spider-tailed viper  -  the tail that fishes for birds
scope: Headline: the spider-tailed horned viper (Pseudocerastes urarachnoides) of western Iran has a tail tip evolved into a lifelike SPIDER — a bulbous 'body' with leg-like scales it wiggles to lure insect-eating birds within striking range. Other distinct wonders: it holds dead still, camouflaged against rock, moving only the tail-lure; the lure specifically fools migrating birds that hunt spiders; it was only described as a distinct species in 2006, one of herpetology's newest showpieces.
source: Bostanchi et al. 2006 (species description); Fathinia et al. field studies documenting caudal-luring behavior and bird predation. Note: fine details of the lure's effectiveness remain an active research topic.
framing_note: Anchor = spider-tailed viper. Lead with the caudal spider-lure (the WHAT?! fact). RESEARCH-HONESTY FLAG: caudal luring is documented on film and in field studies, but frame the lure as observed BEHAVIOR ('it wiggles the tail and birds strike at it') rather than asserting the snake 'knows' it looks like a spider. Distinct rungs: the freeze-and-only-the-tail-moves ambush, the bird-prey target, the recent 2006 description. Real binomial Pseudocerastes urarachnoides.

name: Gaboon viper  -  the longest fangs of any snake
scope: Headline: the Gaboon viper (Bitis gabonica) of central African rainforests grows the longest fangs of any snake — up to about 5 cm (2 inches), folded back against the roof of the mouth until it strikes. Other distinct wonders: a leaf-litter camouflage pattern so precise it's nearly invisible on the forest floor, striking only when prey walks over it; among the largest venom yields of any viper; a slow, sit-and-wait ambush hunter rather than a chaser.
source: African herpetology references; venom-yield and fang-length morphometrics for Bitis gabonica.
framing_note: Anchor = Gaboon viper. Lead with the fang length — a constructed number (2-inch folding fangs, longest of any snake) that passes the Dinner Test because it's superlative-anchored, not a cold stat. Distinct rungs: the leaf-litter camouflage (vivid concealment), the huge venom yield, the ambush strategy. Don't restate 'big fangs' twice. Real binomial Bitis gabonica.

name: Hognose snake  -  the drama-queen death-faker
scope: Headline: the hognose snake (genus Heterodon) fakes death theatrically — it writhes, flips belly-up, gapes its mouth, lolls its tongue, sometimes smears musk and even bleeds from the mouth, then plays limp; flip it right-side-up and it rolls back over as if insisting it's dead. Other distinct wonders: BEFORE the death act, it bluffs the opposite — flattening its neck into a cobra-like hood and hiss-striking (usually with a closed mouth); the upturned 'hognose' snout is a shovel for digging toads out of sand; it's a toad specialist with mild rear-fang venom that subdues toads.
source: North American herpetology; documented thanatosis (death-feigning) behavior in Heterodon.
framing_note: Anchor = hognose. Lead with the theatrical death-feign (the WHAT?! — including the 'roll back over when flipped' detail). Distinct rungs: the cobra-hood BLUFF that precedes it (opposite behavior, vivid), the shovel snout for digging toads (named object + function), the toad-specialist diet. Frame death-feigning as an instinctive behavior, not conscious 'acting.' Genus Heterodon.

name: Flying snake  -  the serpent that glides
scope: Headline: the flying snake (genus Chrysopelea of SE Asia) glides between trees by flattening its whole body into a ribbon and undulating in mid-air, turning itself into a wing. Other distinct wonders: it launches by hanging in a J-shape and flinging itself off the branch; it sucks in its belly and flares its ribs to make a concave, semicircular cross-section that catches air; it keeps side-to-side 'swimming' motions going the entire glide to stay stable — studied with high-speed cameras (Socha).
source: Jake Socha's aerodynamics/biomechanics research on Chrysopelea gliding.
framing_note: Anchor = flying snake. Lead with the glide-by-flattening wonder. Distinct rungs: the J-launch (vivid action), the flattened concave body-shape that acts as a wing (structural fact), the constant undulation in air (counterintuitive). Distinguish clearly from Draco (ribs) and Wallace's frog (webbed feet). Genus Chrysopelea.

name: Armadillo girdled lizard  -  the lizard that bites its own tail
scope: Headline: the armadillo girdled lizard (Ouroborus cataphractus) of South Africa curls into a ball and BITES ITS OWN TAIL, holding the ring so its spiny armored back faces out — the living echo of the ouroboros. Other distinct wonders: rows of heavy, spiky keeled scales cover its body like plate armor; unusually for a lizard it gives live birth and a female typically bears just one or two young; it lives in social groups in rock cracks, unusual reptile sociality.
source: South African herpetology; the genus name Ouroborus was assigned for the tail-biting posture.
framing_note: Anchor = armadillo girdled lizard. Lead with the tail-biting defensive ball (the named ouroboros image — a vivid, memorable handle). Distinct rungs: the spiny plate-armor scales (armor object), the rare-for-a-lizard live birth of 1-2 young (constructed number, surprising), the social rock-crevice groups. Real binomial Ouroborus cataphractus.

name: Shingleback skink  -  the lizard with a tail shaped like its head
scope: Headline: the shingleback skink (Tiliqua rugosa) of Australia has a fat, stumpy tail shaped like its own HEAD — a decoy that confuses predators about which end will bolt, and a fat store for lean times. Other distinct wonders: it mates for life, the same pair reuniting season after season for up to 20 years (rare monogamy in reptiles); when threatened it gapes to flash a startling bright-blue tongue; it bears live young — big, well-developed babies, only one or two per litter.
source: Australian herpetology; long-term Bull et al. studies documenting shingleback pair-bond fidelity.
framing_note: Anchor = shingleback (a.k.a. bobtail/sleepy lizard). Lead with the head-mimic tail (vivid decoy + fat-store double function). Distinct rungs: the lifelong pair-bond (documented up to ~20 years — a genuine WHAT?! for a reptile), the blue-tongue threat display, the live-birth of one or two large young. One wonder per rung. Real binomial Tiliqua rugosa.

name: Mata mata turtle  -  the leaf that vacuums up fish
scope: Headline: the mata mata (Chelus fimbriata) of the Amazon looks exactly like a rotting leaf or piece of bark — a jagged, flap-covered shell and a flat triangular head with skin fringes — so fish swim right up to it. Other distinct wonders: it doesn't bite; it strikes by suddenly opening its huge throat and SUCKING the fish in with a rush of water (gape-and-suck feeding), then spits the water back out; a snorkel-like tube snout lets it breathe at the surface without lifting its head; skin flaps on the neck may sense water movement from prey.
source: South American herpetology; suction-feeding kinematics studies of Chelus.
framing_note: Anchor = mata mata. Lead with the leaf/bark camouflage (vivid concealment). Distinct rungs: the suction strike (vivid mechanism — 'vacuums' the fish, doesn't bite), the snorkel snout (named object + function). Keep mini. Don't restate 'looks like a leaf' twice. Real binomial Chelus fimbriata.

name: Leatherback turtle  -  the warm-blooded reptile giant
scope: Headline: the leatherback (Dermochelys coriacea) is the biggest turtle alive and — extraordinary for a reptile — keeps its body warmer than the freezing water around it (gigantothermy plus heat-exchange plumbing), diving into cold deep water most reptiles couldn't survive. Other distinct wonders: no hard shell — a leathery, ridged, rubbery back instead of bony plates; a throat lined with backward-pointing spines that trap slippery jellyfish, its near-exclusive food; it dives over 1,000 m, deeper than most whales.
source: Marine herpetology; gigantothermy and dive-physiology studies of Dermochelys.
framing_note: Anchor = leatherback. Lead with warm-bodied-in-cold-water (the reptile-rule-breaker wonder). Distinct rungs: the leathery shell (named structure, no bony plates), the spine-lined throat for gripping jellyfish (vivid object + jelly diet), the >1,000 m dive (constructed superlative — deeper than most whales). One wonder per rung. Real binomial Dermochelys coriacea.

name: Surinam toad  -  babies that erupt from the mother's back
scope: Headline: the Surinam toad (Pipa pipa) carries its eggs embedded in the skin of its BACK — the skin grows over each egg into a honeycomb of pockets, the young develop inside, and weeks later fully-formed toadlets pop out through the mother's back. Other distinct wonders: it's flat as a pancake, a floppy leaf-shaped body that hides it on the riverbed; it has no tongue and no teeth — it hunts by lunging and vacuuming prey into its mouth; it has star-tipped fingers with sensory filaments to feel for prey in murky water.
source: Amphibian reproductive-biology literature on Pipa pipa (dermal brooding).
framing_note: Anchor = Surinam toad. Lead with the young-erupt-from-the-back wonder (the ultimate WHAT?! — describe the skin-pocket brooding accurately). Distinct rungs: the pancake-flat leaf body (camouflage), tongueless suction feeding, the star-fingered sensory hands. Keep mini; the back-brooding is the star. Real binomial Pipa pipa.

name: Darwin's frog  -  the father who broods young in his throat
scope: Headline: in Darwin's frog (Rhinoderma darwinii) of Chile and Argentina, the FATHER scoops up the developing eggs and holds them inside his vocal sac, where the tadpoles grow, until fully-formed froglets hop out of his mouth. Other distinct wonders: a pointed leaf-shaped nose and dead-leaf camouflage on the forest floor; when threatened it flops belly-up and lies still, playing dead among the litter; named for Charles Darwin, who collected it on the Beagle voyage — a coherent human-anchored payoff.
source: Amphibian literature on Rhinoderma darwinii vocal-sac brooding; Darwin's Beagle collection records.
framing_note: Anchor = Darwin's frog. Lead with the father-broods-in-vocal-sac wonder (froglets from the mouth). Distinct rungs: the leaf-nose camouflage, the play-dead flop, and ONE human-anchored rung (Darwin collected it on the Beagle) as the coherent payoff, not orphan trivia. Real binomial Rhinoderma darwinii.

name: Hairy frog  -  the frog that breaks its own bones into claws
scope: Headline: the hairy frog (Trichobatrachus robustus) of Cameroon — the 'horror frog' — has no true claws until it's threatened, when it deliberately breaks the bones of its own toes and pushes the sharp broken ends out through its skin to form claws. Other distinct wonders: the 'hair' is not hair — breeding males grow fringes of thin skin flaps (dermal papillae) thought to absorb extra oxygen while the male guards eggs; it's eaten by people in parts of Cameroon, who use spears because handling it risks the claws.
source: Blackburn, Hanken & Jenkins 2008 (Harvard) describing the claw mechanism. Note: exactly how the claw retracts (whether it heals back) is not fully resolved — flag honestly.
framing_note: Anchor = hairy frog. Lead with the break-your-own-bones-into-claws wonder. RESEARCH-HONESTY FLAG: the bone-claw is documented (Blackburn et al. 2008), but whether/how the claw retracts and heals is NOT fully known — the answer should say the extension is documented while the retraction is uncertain, rather than asserting a clean retract-and-heal cycle. Distinct rungs: the 'hair' that is actually oxygen-absorbing skin fringes (correct the name), the spear-hunting human payoff. Real binomial Trichobatrachus robustus.

name: Wallace's flying frog  -  the frog that parachutes on webbed feet
scope: Headline: Wallace's flying frog (Rhacophorus nigropalmatus) of Borneo/Malaysia glides tree-to-tree by spreading four huge, fully webbed feet like parachutes and using flaps of skin along its limbs to catch air. Other distinct wonders: sticky enlarged toe pads let it grip and land on smooth leaves and trunks after a glide; it's a canopy frog that comes down mainly to breed in wallows below; named for Alfred Russel Wallace, co-discoverer of natural selection, who described gliding frogs from the Malay Archipelago — a coherent human payoff.
source: Herpetology of Rhacophorus; Wallace's 'The Malay Archipelago' account of a gliding frog.
framing_note: Anchor = Wallace's flying frog. Lead with the parachute-on-webbed-feet glide. Distinct rungs: the sticky toe pads for landing (object + function), and ONE human-anchored rung (Wallace and the Malay Archipelago) as coherent payoff. Distinguish from Draco (ribs) and flying snake (flattened body). Real binomial Rhacophorus nigropalmatus.

name: Caecilian  -  the legless amphibian whose young eat its skin
scope: Headline: caecilians are amphibians with NO legs — long, ringed, burrowing animals that look like giant earthworms or snakes but are neither. Other distinct wonders: in some species the mother grows a thick, fatty outer skin and the babies peel and EAT it off her with special baby teeth (dermatophagy / skin-feeding); they hunt underground almost blind, with a pair of retractable sensory tentacles between eye and nostril to 'smell-taste' the soil; a few species deliver a mild venom-like toxin from glands near the teeth (recently reported).
source: Amphibian literature on Gymnophiona; Kupfer et al. on maternal dermatophagy; recent reports of oral venom glands (flag as recent/under study).
framing_note: Anchor = caecilian (the group; can name a genus like Boulengerula). Lead with 'legless amphibian, not a worm or snake' (recognition + wonder). Distinct rungs: the babies eating the mother's skin (the WHAT?! — describe dermatophagy accurately, not as cruelty), the sensory tentacle for smelling soil (named organ), the recently-reported oral toxin glands. RESEARCH FLAG: the venom-gland finding is recent and under study — attribute it as a reported finding. One wonder per rung.

name: Olm  -  the blind cave 'baby dragon' that lives a century
scope: Headline: the olm (Proteus anguinus) is a pale, blind amphibian of European cave rivers that villagers once thought was a baby dragon washed up from underground. Other distinct wonders: it lives past 100 years and can go many YEARS between meals in the cold, food-poor cave; it never grows up in the usual way — it keeps external feathery gills its whole life (neoteny, like the axolotl); scientists tracking marked individuals found some barely moved for years, one for over seven years, in a slow cave existence.
source: Cave-biology literature on Proteus anguinus; longevity estimates (Voituron et al.); the dragon-folklore origin as documented natural history.
framing_note: Anchor = olm. Lead with the blind cave 'baby dragon' recognition hook (the folklore is a real historical fact about the animal, fine to tell). Distinct rungs: the ~100-year lifespan + years-without-food (constructed longevity wonder), the lifelong feathery gills / neoteny (named trait, tie to axolotl as convergent), the near-motionless tracked life. One wonder per rung; don't restate 'blind' twice. Real binomial Proteus anguinus.

name: Hellbender  -  the giant 'snot otter' that breathes through wrinkles
scope: Headline: the hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis) of Appalachian streams is North America's biggest salamander — up to ~70 cm — and has almost no working lungs; it breathes through its skin, which is thrown into loose, baggy WRINKLES that hugely increase surface area for absorbing oxygen from cold, fast water. Other distinct wonders: those folds only work in clean, well-oxygenated water, so the hellbender is a living gauge of stream health (silt and pollution suffocate it); the father guards the eggs under a big flat rock; folksy names like 'snot otter' and 'devil dog' — a coherent human-culture payoff.
source: North American herpetology; cutaneous-respiration studies of Cryptobranchus; conservation literature on it as a water-quality indicator.
framing_note: Anchor = hellbender. Lead with the wrinkled-skin skin-breathing wonder (the folds = more surface for oxygen). Distinct rungs: needing clean cold water so it indicates stream health (consequence), the egg-guarding father, and the folk-name payoff ('snot otter') as a coherent hook, not orphan trivia. Real binomial Cryptobranchus alleganiensis.

name: Purple frog  -  the pig-nosed frog that surfaces for two weeks a year
scope: Headline: the purple frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis) of India's Western Ghats spends almost its whole life underground and surfaces for only about two weeks a year to breed with the monsoon rains — so it stayed unknown to science until 2003. Other distinct wonders: a bloated, glossy purple body and a tiny pointed pig-like snout; it eats termites underground through a special groove-and-tongue setup without ever coming up; it's a 'living fossil' whose lineage split from its nearest relatives (in the Seychelles) around the time India was its own island continent — a Gondwana-breakup story anchored on the animal.
source: Biju & Bossuyt 2003 (species description in Nature); molecular-phylogeny work placing it as an ancient Gondwanan lineage.
framing_note: Anchor = purple frog. Lead with the two-weeks-a-year-above-ground / discovered-2003 wonder. Distinct rungs: the pig-nosed purple body (vivid appearance), the underground termite-eating groove, the ancient Gondwana-relict lineage (the deep-time payoff, animal-anchored). Real binomial Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis.

name: Bullet ant  -  the worst sting on the Schmidt index
scope: Headline: the bullet ant (Paraponera clavata) of Central/South American rainforests delivers the most painful insect sting known — Justin Schmidt rated it the top of his sting-pain index, likening it to being shot, with waves of pain lasting for hours. Other distinct wonders: the pain comes from a specific neurotoxin, poneratoxin, that jams nerve signalling; the Satere-Mawe people of Brazil weave dozens of live bullet ants into a glove for a coming-of-age ordeal — a coherent human-anchored payoff; it's a big ant (~2-3 cm) that nests at tree bases and forages up into the canopy.
source: Justin Schmidt's sting-pain index and 'The Sting of the Wild'; poneratoxin pharmacology; ethnographic accounts of the Satere-Mawe glove ritual.
framing_note: Anchor = bullet ant. Lead with the #1-on-Schmidt sting (Schmidt is a NAMED thing — the index and the man are the memorable handle). Distinct rungs: the named toxin poneratoxin and what it does to nerves (mechanism), the Satere-Mawe glove ritual (coherent human payoff, describe respectfully as a real cultural practice), the ant's size/nest. One wonder per rung. Real binomial Paraponera clavata.

name: Velvet ant  -  the 'cow killer' that is really a wasp
scope: Headline: the velvet ant (family Mutillidae) is not an ant at all — the fuzzy, brightly-coloured 'ant' is a wingless female WASP, and its sting is so fierce it earned the name 'cow killer.' Other distinct wonders: it's armored like a tank — an exoskeleton so hard collectors struggle to pin it and predators struggle to bite through; it squeaks (stridulates) a warning when grabbed; the female is a parasite that sneaks into other bees' and wasps' nests to lay eggs on their young.
source: Mutillidae entomology; Schmidt sting notes; studies of velvet-ant exoskeleton hardness and stridulation.
framing_note: Anchor = velvet ant. Lead with 'not an ant — a wingless female wasp' (the recognition-flip wonder; 'cow killer' is the memorable name). Distinct rungs: the near-unbreakable armored exoskeleton, the warning squeak (stridulation), the parasitic nest-invading lifestyle. Family Mutillidae (can name Dasymutilla for the classic US 'cow killer').

name: Trap-jaw ant  -  jaws that snap faster than almost anything alive
scope: Headline: the trap-jaw ant (genus Odontomachus) has spring-loaded jaws it cocks wide open and snaps shut in well under a millisecond — among the fastest movements in the animal kingdom, clocked over 60 m/s. Other distinct wonders: it can fire those jaws against the ground to CATAPULT its whole body into the air, backflipping away from danger (an 'escape jump'); trigger hairs inside the jaws release the latch the instant prey touches them; the same jaws serve as both a lethal snap-trap on prey and an ejector seat.
source: Patek, Baio & Fisher high-speed studies of Odontomachus jaw kinematics and escape-jumping.
framing_note: Anchor = trap-jaw ant. Lead with the fastest-snapping-jaws wonder (constructed superlative). Distinct rungs: the jaw-powered escape backflip (vivid action — the SAME structure, DIFFERENT use, so it's a distinct wonder not a restated headline), the trigger hairs that release the latch (mechanism). Genus Odontomachus.

name: Honeypot ant  -  living storage jars for the colony
scope: Headline: in honeypot ant colonies (e.g. genus Myrmecocystus), special workers called repletes are fed until their abdomens swell into round, translucent, honey-filled globes the size of a grape — living storage jars hanging from the nest ceiling. Other distinct wonders: nestmates 'milk' them by stroking their mouthparts, and the repletes regurgitate stored food to feed the colony through droughts; they hang motionless upside down for months, too swollen to walk; some desert peoples dig them up and eat the sweet abdomens as a natural candy — a coherent human payoff.
source: Desert-ant entomology on Myrmecocystus repletes; ethnographic records of honeypot-ant foraging by Aboriginal Australians and others.
framing_note: Anchor = honeypot ant. Lead with the living-storage-jar replete (the swollen honey-globe abdomen). Distinct rungs: nestmates milking them / feeding the colony in drought (function), the immobile upside-down hanging life, the human bush-food payoff. Describe respectfully. Genus Myrmecocystus (or note Australian Camponotus honeypots).

name: Jewel wasp  -  the wasp that turns a cockroach into a zombie
scope: Headline: the emerald jewel wasp (Ampulex compressa) stings a cockroach TWICE — the second sting goes precisely into the roach's brain, injecting venom that switches off its escape drive so it can't flee even though it can still walk. Other distinct wonders: the wasp then grabs an antenna and LEADS the docile roach on a walk to its burrow like a dog on a leash; it lays an egg on the roach and the larva eats the still-living, un-fleeing roach from inside; the venom targets specific brain regions controlling the escape reflex — a precise neuro-hijack, not general poison.
source: Frederic Libersat's neurobiology of Ampulex compressa venom and the cockroach escape circuit.
framing_note: Anchor = jewel wasp (tell it as the wasp's hunting story, roach as prey). Lead with the brain-sting that kills the escape reflex (the WHAT?!). Distinct rungs: leading the zombie roach by the antenna (vivid action), the larva eating it alive from inside, the precision of the venom on the escape circuit (mechanism). Describe the neuro-hijack as documented behavior, not narrated cruelty. Real binomial Ampulex compressa.

name: Tarantula hawk  -  the wasp that hunts tarantulas
scope: Headline: the tarantula hawk (genus Pepsis) is a giant wasp that hunts TARANTULAS — it stings the spider to paralyze it, then drags the living-but-frozen tarantula, often many times its own weight, into a burrow. Other distinct wonders: it lays a single egg on the paralyzed spider and the larva eats it alive over weeks, saving the vital organs for last so the food stays fresh; its own sting rates near the very top of the Schmidt pain index (second only to the bullet ant) — Schmidt's advice was basically 'lie down and scream'; adults are harmless nectar-drinkers, the hunting is only for the young.
source: Pepsini entomology; Schmidt sting-index notes on Pepsis.
framing_note: Anchor = tarantula hawk. Lead with 'a wasp that hunts tarantulas' (the WHAT?! matchup). Distinct rungs: paralyze-and-bury with the larva eating the spider alive (organs last), the near-top Schmidt sting (Schmidt's named quote as the handle), the twist that adults just sip nectar. Distinguish clearly from the jewel wasp (that's a roach and a brain-sting). Genus Pepsis.

name: Bolas spider  -  the spider that fishes with a glue ball
scope: Headline: the bolas spider (genus Mastophora) doesn't build a web — it dangles a single silk thread tipped with a sticky glue ball and swings it like a cowboy's bolas to snag flying moths out of the air. Other distinct wonders: it doesn't just wait — it releases a chemical MIMIC of female moth pheromone, luring male moths of specific species straight to the swinging glue ball; different bolas species tune their fake perfume to whatever moths are flying that season; by day it sits still disguised as a bird dropping.
source: Eberhard and Yeargan studies of Mastophora bolas-swinging and aggressive pheromone chemical mimicry.
framing_note: Anchor = bolas spider. Lead with the fishing-with-a-glue-ball wonder (vivid action). Distinct rungs: the fake-pheromone lure that pulls male moths in (the WHAT?! chemical mimicry — a DISTINCT fact from the swing), tuning the scent to seasonal moths, the bird-dropping daytime disguise. Genus Mastophora.

name: Ogre-faced spider  -  the net-caster that throws its web
scope: Headline: the ogre-faced (net-casting) spider (genus Deinopis) holds a small stretchy web between its front legs and THROWS it over passing prey like a fisherman casting a net, then snaps it back over the victim. Other distinct wonders: it has two enormous forward-facing eyes — among the largest simple eyes of any spider — giving it superb night vision to aim in near-darkness; recent research shows it can HEAR — it catches flying insects by detecting their wingbeat sounds through leg sensors and flips backward to net them out of the air; by day it stretches out thin as a twig to hide.
source: Deinopis vision studies (Stafstrom); Stafstrom et al. 2021 on airborne prey capture via hearing. Flag the hearing finding as recent.
framing_note: Anchor = ogre-faced spider. Lead with the throw-the-net hunting (vivid action). Distinct rungs: the huge night-vision eyes (named feature — the 'ogre face'), the RECENT finding that it hears wingbeats and nets flying prey (flag as a 2021 finding), the twig disguise. One wonder per rung. Genus Deinopis.

name: Diving bell spider  -  the spider that lives underwater in a bubble
scope: Headline: the diving bell spider (Argyroneta aquatica) is the only spider that spends its whole life UNDERWATER — it spins a dome of silk between water plants and fills it with air carried down as a shimmering bubble on its body, making a diving bell it lives, eats, and mates inside. Other distinct wonders: the silk bell works like a gill — oxygen from the water diffuses IN and carbon dioxide diffuses OUT, so the spider can stay submerged for a day or more without resurfacing; the bubble on its body makes it look silvery, which gives it the name Argyroneta ('silver net'); males are unusually larger than females, opposite the spider norm, likely because they swim to hunt.
source: Seymour & Hetz 2011 showing the air bell functions as a physical gill; European aquatic-arachnid literature.
framing_note: Anchor = diving bell spider. Lead with the lives-underwater-in-an-air-bubble wonder. Distinct rungs: the bell working as a GILL (oxygen diffuses in — the mechanism, a distinct fact from just 'has a bubble'), the silvery bubble giving it its silver-net name, the reversed male-larger sizing. Real binomial Argyroneta aquatica.

name: Goliath birdeater  -  the biggest spider on Earth
scope: Headline: the Goliath birdeater (Theraphosa blondi) of South America is the world's biggest spider by mass — a leg-span up to ~30 cm, body the size of a fist. Other distinct wonders: despite the name it rarely eats birds — it mostly takes worms, insects and small vertebrates on the forest floor; its main defense isn't the bite but flicking clouds of tiny barbed, itching hairs (urticating setae) off its abdomen at attackers; when threatened it makes a hissing sound by rubbing leg bristles together (stridulation), audible several metres away.
source: Theraphosidae entomology; size records and urticating-hair defense literature for Theraphosa blondi.
framing_note: Anchor = Goliath birdeater. Lead with 'biggest spider on Earth' (constructed superlative + fist-size handle). Distinct rungs: the misleading name — it rarely eats birds (myth-correction), the flicked itching-hair defense (vivid, named urticating setae), the audible leg-bristle hiss. Real binomial Theraphosa blondi.

name: Giant weta  -  the heavyweight insect of New Zealand
scope: Headline: the giant weta (genus Deinacrida) of New Zealand is one of the heaviest insects alive — a big female can outweigh a sparrow, tipping over 70 g. Other distinct wonders: it survived because New Zealand had no land mammals, so wetas filled the mouse-and-rat niche as nocturnal ground foragers ('the invertebrate mouse') — and now rats threaten them; when frightened it doesn't bite but rears up, spreads its huge spiny back legs and kicks them outward in a warning; some alpine wetas freeze nearly solid in winter and thaw back to life come spring.
source: New Zealand entomology on Deinacrida; the record heavy specimen; alpine-weta freeze-tolerance studies.
framing_note: Anchor = giant weta. Lead with 'one of the heaviest insects — heavier than a sparrow' (constructed superlative). Distinct rungs: the mammal-free-NZ backstory (why it got big — the invertebrate mouse), the spiny back-leg kick display, the alpine-species freeze-and-thaw. Keep DISTINCT from the tree-lobster stick insect (separate ladder). Genus Deinacrida.

name: Lord Howe tree lobster  -  the stick insect back from the dead
scope: Headline: the Lord Howe Island stick insect (Dryococelus australis), the 'tree lobster,' was declared EXTINCT after rats ate them all out by the 1920s — then in 2001 climbers found about two dozen survivors clinging to a single bush on Ball's Pyramid, a bare sea-stack 20 km away. Other distinct wonders: it's a huge, heavy, glossy-black stick insect as long as a hand, far bulkier than a normal stick insect (hence 'tree lobster'); those few survivors were bred back — a captive population founded largely from one pair, 'Adam and Eve'; pairs sleep coiled together, the male draping legs over the female, unusual tenderness for an insect.
source: Lord Howe stick-insect rediscovery accounts (2001 Ball's Pyramid); Melbourne Zoo captive-breeding program records.
framing_note: Anchor = Lord Howe tree lobster. Lead with the extinct-then-rediscovered-on-a-sea-stack wonder (the WHAT?! comeback story — the animal's own narrative). Distinct rungs: the hand-long heavy 'tree lobster' body, the breed-back from 'Adam and Eve', the coiled-together sleeping pairs. Distinct ladder from the giant weta. Real binomial Dryococelus australis.

name: Orchid mantis  -  the flower that eats the pollinator
scope: Headline: the orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) of SE Asia has legs shaped and coloured like pink-and-white petals, so it looks like a blossom — and insects fly TO it thinking it's a flower. Other distinct wonders: research (O'Hanlon) showed it doesn't even need to sit on a real flower; it is MORE attractive to pollinators than many real blooms — a rare case of an animal being a 'better flower' than the flowers, luring prey rather than just hiding; young nymphs add a red-and-black ant-mimicking look for extra disguise; it changes shade paler or darker to match its surroundings.
source: O'Hanlon, Holwell & Herberstein 2014 demonstrating aggressive floral mimicry (prey lured, not just camouflaged) in Hymenopus coronatus.
framing_note: Anchor = orchid mantis. Lead with the petal-shaped legs / looks-like-a-flower wonder. Distinct rungs: the RESEARCH twist that it lures pollinators better than real flowers do (aggressive mimicry, a distinct fact from just 'looks like a flower' — cite O'Hanlon 2014), the ant-mimic nymph stage, the colour-shifting. One wonder per rung. Real binomial Hymenopus coronatus.

name: Treehopper  -  the insect with alien headgear
scope: Headline: treehoppers (family Membracidae) grow bizarre, oversized structures on their backs — the enlarged pronotum sculpted into thorns, antlers, balls, or shapes that look like alien helmets or bits of the plant. Other distinct wonders: many are thorn mimics — a row of them on a stem looks exactly like the plant's spines, hiding them in plain sight; they suck plant sap and dribble sugary honeydew that ANTS farm, guarding the treehoppers from predators in exchange for the sweet reward; some mothers stand guard over their eggs and nymphs and buzz vibrations through the stem to warn the young of danger.
source: Membracidae entomology; pronotum morphology; treehopper-ant mutualism and maternal vibrational communication (Cocroft) studies.
framing_note: Anchor = treehopper. Lead with the outlandish helmet/thorn headgear (the enlarged pronotum — vivid object). Distinct rungs: the thorn-mimic row-on-a-stem disguise (concealment), the ant-farming honeydew mutualism (relationship), the vibrating guardian mother. Family Membracidae. Don't restate 'weird shape on its back' twice.

name: Atlas moth  -  one of the biggest moths, with snake-head wingtips
scope: Headline: the atlas moth (Attacus atlas) of Asia is among the largest moths on Earth, a wingspan up to ~27 cm and more total wing area than almost any insect. Other distinct wonders: the curved, patterned wingtips look startlingly like a COBRA'S HEAD — when disturbed the moth flaps so the 'snake heads' seem to strike, scaring off predators; the adult has NO working mouth and never eats — it lives only a week or two on fat stored as a caterpillar, existing just to mate and lay eggs; in parts of Asia its tough silk (fagara) is spun into a coarse brown cloth — a coherent human payoff.
source: Saturniidae entomology on Attacus atlas; size and wing-area figures; fagara-silk textile use.
framing_note: Anchor = atlas moth. Lead with 'one of the biggest moths' (superlative + wing-area handle). Distinct rungs: the cobra-head wingtip mimicry (vivid defense), the mouthless adult that never eats and lives ~a week (jaw-dropping consequence), the fagara-silk human payoff. Real binomial Attacus atlas.

name: Antlion  -  the larva that digs a sand death-trap
scope: Headline: the antlion larva digs a perfect cone-shaped pit in loose sand and buries itself at the bottom with only its jaws showing — an ant that slips over the edge slides down the crumbling walls straight into those jaws. Other distinct wonders: if prey scrambles at the rim, the larva FLICKS sand up at it with its head to knock it back down into the pit; it walks only backward, spiralling to dig the pit by throwing out sand; the fierce trap-digging larva grows up into a delicate, harmless, lacewing-like flying adult almost nobody recognizes as the same animal.
source: Myrmeleontidae entomology; pit-building and prey-capture behavior studies.
framing_note: Anchor = antlion. Lead with the sand-cone death-trap (vivid structure + hunting). Distinct rungs: flicking sand to knock prey down (vivid action, distinct from just 'has a pit'), the backward-only walking that builds the pit, the transformation into the unrecognizable lacewing-like adult. Family Myrmeleontidae.

name: New Zealand glowworm  -  the larva that fishes with glowing lines
scope: Headline: the New Zealand glowworm (Arachnocampa luminosa) is a fly LARVA that hangs sticky silk fishing lines from a cave ceiling and glows blue-green at the end of its body to lure flying insects into the sticky threads. Other distinct wonders: ceilings packed with thousands of them look exactly like a starry night sky (the famous Waitomo caves) — a coherent tourism/human handle; the glow is a chemical light (bioluminescence) and a hungrier larva glows BRIGHTER to lure more prey; the beautiful lines are traps — trapped insects are reeled up and eaten, and the adult fly that finally hatches has no mouth and lives only days to mate.
source: Arachnocampa luminosa entomology; bioluminescence and snare-line predation studies; Waitomo natural history.
framing_note: Anchor = NZ glowworm. Lead with 'a fly larva that fishes with glowing sticky lines' (the WHAT?! — it's a maggot, not a worm; correct gently). Distinct rungs: the starry-sky cave ceilings (Waitomo, the human/place handle), the hunger-brightens-the-glow lure detail, the mouthless short-lived adult. Real binomial Arachnocampa luminosa. Keep DISTINCT from firefly (that's its own ladder elsewhere).

name: Assassin bug  -  the ambush hunter that wears its victims
scope: Headline: assassin bugs (family Reduviidae) stab prey with a sharp curved beak (the rostrum), inject saliva that liquefies the victim's insides, and drink it out like a milkshake. Other distinct wonders: one kind (the acanthaspidine/'masked hunter' relatives) piles the drained CORPSES of its prey onto its own back as camouflage and armor, walking around wearing a heap of dead ants; the feather-legged assassin lures ants by offering a gland secretion, then grabs them; a few (kissing bugs) feed on blood and can carry Chagas disease — a factual, non-lurid health note.
source: Reduviidae entomology; corpse-carrying camouflage in assassin-bug nymphs; feather-legged assassin luring; kissing-bug/Chagas basics.
framing_note: Anchor = assassin bug. Lead with the stab-and-liquefy-and-drink beak feeding (vivid mechanism). Distinct rungs: the nymph that stacks its victims' corpses on its back as a disguise (the WHAT?!), the ant-luring feather-legged kind, and a plain factual kissing-bug/Chagas rung (state it neutrally, no fear-mongering). Family Reduviidae. One wonder per rung.

name: Velvet worm  -  the glue-cannon hunter of the forest floor
scope: Headline: the velvet worm (phylum Onychophora) hunts by firing two jets of instant-setting GLUE from nozzles beside its mouth, spraying a net of sticky slime over prey from a few centimetres away. Other distinct wonders: it's a living link — soft, legged, and neither worm nor insect nor arthropod, a survivor of a lineage over 500 million years old (Cambrian-style body plan); it walks on many stubby, clawed, fluid-filled leg-stumps and oozes forward slowly in the dark leaf litter; some species live in family groups with a social pecking order, unusual for such an ancient, simple-looking animal.
source: Onychophoran biology; slime-jet mechanics (Concha et al.); Cambrian-relatives and lobopodian body-plan literature.
framing_note: Anchor = velvet worm. Lead with the glue-cannon slime-jet hunting (vivid, mechanical wonder). Distinct rungs: the deep-time 'living link' identity (neither worm nor arthropod, ~500-My lineage — the wonder is what it IS), the stubby clawed leg-stump walking, the social family groups. Phylum Onychophora. Don't call it a worm or insect as fact.

name: Zombie-ant fungus  -  the carpenter ant's fate
scope: Headline (told as the ANT's story): a healthy carpenter ant (Camponotus) picks up spores of a fungus (Ophiocordyceps unilateralis); the fungus grows through the ant and, near death, drives the ant to leave its trail, climb to a precise height on a leaf, and lock its jaws onto a leaf vein in a 'death grip' before it dies. Other distinct wonders: the fungus makes the ant bite at a spot with just the right temperature and humidity for the fungus to grow — the same height and orientation again and again ('graveyards' of gripping dead ants); after the ant dies a stalk erupts from its head and rains spores down onto the trail below to catch the next ants; research shows the fungus controls the ant's MUSCLES directly and largely spares the brain — a body-hijack, not a mind read from inside the skull.
source: David Hughes / Charissa de Bekker research on Ophiocordyceps unilateralis; Fredericksen et al. 2017 showing muscle invasion with the brain largely intact.
framing_note: Anchor = the carpenter ant (tell it as the ANT's story, per the task). ACCURACY-CRITICAL: the controller is a FUNGUS (Ophiocordyceps), not a virus or a 'zombie disease' — name it correctly and never anthropomorphize the fungus as a conscious puppeteer. Lead with the death-grip climb-and-bite. Distinct rungs: the precise height/temperature/humidity of the bite (why there), the spore-stalk from the head raining onto the trail, and the RESEARCH finding that the fungus works the muscles while largely sparing the brain (flag as Fredericksen et al. 2017 — a body-hijack, corrects the 'mind control' cliche). One wonder per rung. Real binomials Camponotus / Ophiocordyceps unilateralis.

name: Vinegaroon  -  the whip scorpion that sprays vinegar
scope: Headline: the vinegaroon (whip scorpion, order Thelyphonida) has no sting and no venom — when threatened it swivels its tail and sprays a fine acid mist that smells sharply of VINEGAR (it's largely acetic acid) at the attacker. Other distinct wonders: the 'tail' is not a stinger at all but a thin whip-like sensory feeler (the flagellum) it waves to feel its way in the dark; it grabs prey with a pair of heavy, spiny, crushing pincer-arms (pedipalps) instead of biting with venom; the mother carries her white eggs and then her hatchlings on her back until they can fend for themselves.
source: Thelyphonida arachnology; acetic-acid defensive-spray chemistry; whip-scorpion maternal-care behavior.
framing_note: Anchor = vinegaroon. Lead with the vinegar-spray defense (no venom — vivid, named acetic-acid mist). Distinct rungs: the whip 'tail' being a sensory feeler not a stinger (correct the scary look), the crushing pincer-arms it uses instead of venom, the egg/hatchling-carrying mother. Order Thelyphonida (a.k.a. Uropygi). One wonder per rung.

name: Why the ice-age giants died  -  overkill vs. climate
scope: Anchored on the ANIMALS: which Pleistocene giants vanished and when — woolly mammoth, mastodon, Smilodon (sabre-tooth), giant ground sloth, glyptodon, Irish elk, woolly rhino, short-faced bear, dire wolf — most gone across the Americas and northern Eurasia roughly 50,000-10,000 years ago as the last ice age ended. The CONTESTED question: WHY. Side 1 (overkill): Paul Martin's 1967 hypothesis that spreading human hunters wiped out slow-breeding megafauna — evidence includes extinctions closely tracking human arrival on continent after continent (and later on islands), and butchered/kill sites. Side 2 (climate): the extinctions coincide with rapid warming, collapsing 'mammoth steppe' habitat, and vegetation turnover as the ice sheets retreated — evidence includes populations crashing with climate swings and some giants outliving humans in refuges. Also flag: many scientists now favor a COMBINATION (climate stress plus human pressure), and the debate is genuinely unresolved.
source: Paul S. Martin 1967 'Prehistoric Overkill' and later work; climate-driven extinction literature (Nogues-Bravo, Cooper, Stuart); combination/synergy models; dated extinction records for named megafauna.
framing_note: CONTESTED — vision_mandated. BOTH SIDES, NO VERDICT: the bank must NOT declare overkill or climate the winner. Frame the WHY as a genuine open scientific debate. Attribute the overkill hypothesis to Paul Martin (1967) as a NAMED position and the climate case to its evidence, present the strongest form of EACH, and include a rung noting many researchers now favor a combined climate+human explanation and that it remains unresolved. Keep every rung ANIMAL-anchored: name the actual giants (mammoth, Smilodon, glyptodon, Irish elk, ground sloth), what vanished, when, and the physical evidence (kill sites, dated remains, habitat/vegetation change) — NOT an abstract policy argument. Contested-question stems must present the claim as a character's/school's position, choices as competing scientific reasoning moves, never impose a yes/no. Accurate dates and real taxa only.
